claims.text: Controlled nanoscale phase separation or local atomic clustering enhances a cooperative magnetic transition in rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys.
The cooperative magnetic transition produces a strong magnetocaloric response at low applied fields.
Nanoscale phase separation or clustering preserves rapid heat exchange.
Nanoscale phase separation or clustering preserves low magnetic hysteresis.
Nanoscale phase separation or clustering preserves mechanical stability.
A controlled annealing and quenching treatment can induce a deliberate degree of nanoscale phase separation or clustering.
Nanoscale phase-separated regions mediate local magnetic exchange interactions.
Nanoscale heterogeneities reduce local magnetic anisotropy.
Reduced local magnetic anisotropy enables a cooperative magnetic transition.
The cooperative magnetic transition increases the isothermal entropy change and adiabatic temperature change.
Interfaces associated with nanoscale heterogeneities facilitate rapid thermal transport.
Interfaces associated with nanoscale heterogeneities help maintain mechanical robustness.
Relative to a homogeneous baseline, the treated alloy will exhibit a larger adiabatic temperature change under a low applied field.
Relative to a homogeneous baseline, the treated alloy will exhibit a larger isothermal entropy change under a low applied field.
Relative to a homogeneous baseline, the treated alloy will exhibit unchanged or reduced magnetic hysteresis.
Relative to a homogeneous baseline, the treated alloy will retain steady mechanical properties.
The proposed effect is expected near the magnetic ordering temperature at applied fields of roughly 1 T.
The proposed effect is limited to compositions and thermal treatments that produce a controllable, moderate degree of nanoscale phase separation.
Failure of increased phase separation to produce a statistically significant increase in either ΔT or ΔS relative to the homogeneous control would falsify the hypothesis.
A correlation between increased phase separation and either greater hysteresis or mechanical degradation would falsify the hypothesis.
